utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. There are a few preliminary matters I'd like to deal with. One that is protective measures for Witness RM021. On the 23rd of August, the Prosecution filed its submission on protective measures for Witness RM021 and in light of the fact that the witness is scheduled to testify later this week, the Chamber invites the Defence to make oral submissions in response to this filing. But perhaps it's better done in private session. Are you able to respond, Mr. Lukic? If not, if you're not able to do it straight away, then please tell us when you expect to be able to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do not object to protective measures for this witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Having dealt with that item, the Chamber was informed that the Prosecution wanted to raise a few matters as well. Meanwhile I put on the record that the Chamber received a short report by the Deputy Registrar on the health issue that was -- that came up last Friday and we also received an update on the health condition of Mr. Mladic dated the 23rd August by the medical officer of the UNDU, Dr. van Gellicum. That's hereby put on the record. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just with respect to that, the Prosecution has not received a copy and would certainly appreciate a copy of that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we only received it this -- I received it only this morning but I take it that it's been filed now which may explain why you haven't seen anything. It mainly refers to a brief examination and then nothing new appeared there, that is a very short summary. Mr. Groome, the Prosecution or, Ms. Bibles, you wanted to raise a -- one or more preliminary matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. And good morning, Your Honours and counsel. There are three brief matters to raise. First, with respect to P01987, the B/C/S translation of this report by Dusan Janc has been uploaded into e-court under document ID number X0240734-B/C/S. We would ask that the Court Officer be instructed to attach it to the English original and for its admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Registrar is instructed in accordance with your request. Next question?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we advise that the corrections to the following exhibits have been made as requested by the Trial Chamber in its decision on Prosecution's bar table motion for the admission of intercepts Srebrenica segment dated 2 May 2013. The Prosecution will seek admission of Exhibit P01414, P1415, and P1416 which is under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do you want to make any submissions on the matter or could we deal with it in the following way: It's a correction which was requested by the Chamber, that we decide to admit and that you have an opportunity to revisit the matter within the next 48 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then P1414 is admitted into evidence, the same for P1415, and P1416 is admitted into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Finally, Your Honour, the Prosecution will seek permission to replace the English translation of P1515 with a revised translation attached, and this situation arose during the testimony of Momir Nikolic who testified at T11958 and 11960 regarding initials at the bottom of a report. The document ID number is 00663720-ET. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I do understand that it's mainly the initials at the bottom which were not reflected rightly in the English version. I would suggest that we take the same position, Mr. Lukic, that the Chamber hereby gives leave to replace the English translation of P1515 with the revised translation as mentioned by Ms. Bibles a second ago, and if there is any need to revisit the matter that you have an opportunity to do so within the next 48 hours. The Registry is instructed to replace the English translation of P1515 as suggested by Ms. Bibles. Nothing else? Then we could -- Mr. Lukic, nothing from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was thinking a bit reluctantly to raise with Your Honours again the issue of four-day week because I don't think we have to be not only humane, we have to be realistic. We will not be able to go five days a week with the health condition in which Mr. Mladic is in right now. We will probably encounter the same situation we had the last week if we continue to push five day week. We saw that even after three weeks of rest, he wasn't able to go through the whole week without having medical problems. Now, after the working week behind us, it's even more likely that we could encounter problems. I don't wish it, but I really envisage it and it's really realistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber will consider the matter. As you may have noticed in the past, the Chamber has always very seriously analysed any medical report which would support your application. We'll continue to do the same. At this moment, may I take it that your request is based on the medical report we have received until now including the ones we received Friday and was -- will be filed today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I haven't seen one from Friday, Your Honours, I don't know from which time is that report. Is it afternoon or morning report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it we have -- Friday we received a report from the Deputy Registrar, as I said before. I will -- that report of Friday, the medical report itself, which I just referred to, will be filed today. So if you want to rely on that any further during the days to come to give a further support to your request, then of course you have an opportunity to do so. The medical report I think I read the title, it's dated the 23rd of August, 2013. It is authored by Ernst-Jan van Gellicum, medical officer UNDU, ICTY, and it contains an introduction, a -- three separate paragraphs and then a conclusion. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm informed that it has been filed by now, Mr. Lukic. It was filed confidentially. If there are no other preliminaries, is the Defence ready to continue its cross-examination? And could you give us an indication, Mr. Lukic, as to how much time you'd still need while the witness is brought in?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope I will be able to finish today, although I have more time left since I used only two hours, 45 minutes in last two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But finish today, it's your expectation that you would need the full morning session?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's my expectation, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm indebted to the Chamber to discuss the letter that Judge Orie asked me whether I had it, and my source was a transcript. So in view of that, I have distributed copies of the transcript both to the booths and to the panel of Judges. I don't know if you need it to have it in front of you and perhaps I can request some assistance in that respect. In the lower part, as you can see, this is a Mladic transcript, pages 15568, and I asked you something from line 21, about your openly expressing your conviction that Slobodan Milosevic was guilty of what he had been charged with, and you said, probably I don't have a specific recollection of saying those words, but I would not be surprised if I had. And then on the next page, 15569, lines 1 through 5, in answer to my question that -- about 50 something persons signed the letter, you said that you remember signing the letter, but I don't specifically recall the contents of the letter. And that this letter including a conclusion that Slobodan Milosevic was guilty. In the upper part of the page, I have pasted part of the transcript from the Perisic case, page 1771 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said, "And that this letter including a conclusion that Slobodan Milosevic was guilty." Where does it say so?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In our transcript, page 15569.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we should, if you are referring to the last two and a half lines, it reads: "I don't -- I don't specifically recall the contents of that letter as including the conclusion that Slobodan Milosevic was guilty." Which I understand, my knowledge of the English language, but I'm ready to be corrected, that the witness doesn't know whether that letter said that Mr. Milosevic was guilty or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's how I thought I was translating it. I agree with you 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see. Yes, because the language is slightly -- yes, perhaps the problem is that in the transcript, the line where it says, "I don't specifically recall the contents of the letter," and then it gives a full stop, and that this letter including a conclusion, is perhaps even more ambiguous as the transcript is so therefore we have a shared understanding of what the transcript says and what it means, that is that the witness does not remember whether it includes or not a conclusion that Mr. Milosevic was guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. I'm sorry if we --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I should have read it in English so we wouldn't have any mistake in translations. But I will correct myself and now I will quote from page 1771 from Perisic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's from line 20, it says: "Q. With regard to your views on, for example, Slobodan Milosevic, you have a definite view with regard to his criminal responsibility, do you not? "A. Yes, I do. "Q. You believe that he's guilty of the crimes for which he was charged, don't you?" Answer, on the next page, line 1: "Yes. "Q. That is a view that you have, as a matter of fact, articulated on more than one occasion? "A. Yes. "Q. That is a view that you have as a matter of fact and we may discuss it later, you have actually sent at least one letter concerning your position about the judgement that was rendered by the International Court of Justice as being a political decision because they didn't use certain information. "A. I don't believe I sent a letter. "Q. You signed a letter that was sent by 54 -- you and 54 of your colleagues; do you recall that? "A. Yes. "Q. And in that letter you made it very clear that in your estimation, Milosevic was guilty. "A. Yes. "Q. And you also made it very clear that as far as you were concerned, the judgement finding -- the finding of that Court was a political decision that, as a matter of fact, avoided what you believed to be compelling evidence that should have brought them to a different position. "A. Yes." [Interpretation] Doctor, has this refreshed your recollection as to the effect that you had signed the letter in which it is unambiguously stated and an estimation was made that Slobodan Milosevic was guilty as stated in both the questions and answers in lines 14 to 16 on page 1772 of the Perisic case transcript?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I still don't have a copy of the letter before me, and I certainly acknowledge that here I concurred that he had been -- I stated that he had been guilty of the crimes for which he was charged in our estimation, that is the estimation of the letter writers. But I don't see the letter, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, have you dealt with this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because what confuses me is to link the guilt of Mr. Milosevic to a decision of the International Court of Justice, where it is, I think, clear to everyone that the International Court of Justice does not express itself on the individual criminal responsibility of persons but on the responsibility of states, and therefore I'm slightly confused by the issue being linked or at least mingled or I don't know exactly; that's the reason why perhaps reading the letter might be relevant for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you want to finalise your concern with the witness or I should?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well of course having expressed this, if you want to -- I could ask the witness how he views the issue I raised, but if you have any specific questions on the matter, Mr. Lukic, I will gladly leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, this statement of yours or expression of views on the guilt of Mr. Milosevic, since it is said that he was guilty, and you have confirmed this, that you and the other people who signed this letter with you, was maintained as a position, can you tell us to whom was this letter addressed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I get concerned when your questions tend to embellish the evidence of the witness. The witness said in their estimation and now when you say that you have confirmed this, since it is said that he was guilty and you have confirmed this, I thought the witness clearly stated that that's their estimation. Quite apart from what Judge Orie has said about what the ICJ's mandate is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I thought, Your Honour, that the witness confirmed today that he remembers signing the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Confirming the letter is one thing. Confirming Mladic's guilt is another.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Milosevic's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I'm sorry, Mr. Mladic. Confirming Milosevic's guilt is quite another. This is what you are saying in the question that you are putting to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll start from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, first of all, to whom did you send the letter in question? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When writing this letter, and whilst you were discussing Mr. Milosevic's guilt, what did you have in mind? Did you have in mind the indictment issued by this Tribunal or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let me be clear. I had no role in drafting the letter. I endorse it on a web page after it had been drafted and signed by several other people. The subject of the letter was the International Court of Justice's decision not to subpoena the full Supreme Defence Council minutes for its consideration of the case before it. It didn't really have any -- as I recall, it didn't have any specific reference to the work of this Tribunal. But I -- again, without looking at it, it's been a good number of years since I have seen it, and would certainly want to have it in front of me before I speculate any further about what it said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you sign this letter before or after you testified in the Milosevic case, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was -- I'm not certain. No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like now to go through to what you said in examination-in-chief. On Thursday, 22nd of August, you said the following and I'm going to read in order to avoid any mistakes. We need page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could -- could the parties agree on that the decision by the ICJ was delivered far after Mr. Milosevic had died and therefore that the letter could not have been signed before giving testimony in the Milosevic case. I'm just trying to reconstruct recent history. Would the parties agree on that so that we have --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So therefore it was a matter easily to be agreed upon. Does this refresh your recollection by any way, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was what I recalled but wasn't certain, so I didn't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we were discussing about P2003 which is your report, there is mention of six strategic goals. We saw that a long time before the publication in the Official Gazette of these goals, they had been discussed at an assembly session. Do you know why it took almost a year and a half for what has been laid down as the strategic goals to publish them in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after the discussion in the assembly session, within the next day or two, there was a further discussion in which the key leaders of the SDS actually disagreed about whether they should be published. Krajisnik, Mr. Krajisnik, favoured publishing them. And Karadzic and others were opposed. I think that they felt this was not something - that is Karadzic and his supporters on this - felt this was not something they wanted publicly known at this time, but there was of course the other side of that, which was that it clearly articulated their ambitions and aims and was useful for that purpose in the peace process. So it's my understanding that they shared the goals with a few of the key negotiators in the peace process but refrained from publishing them publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, one correction for the transcript. You said, "P2003 which is your report," but that is not the report of the witness. P2003 is the Official Gazette where the strategic goals were published.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, and thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Being unpublished the public was not aware of it, the broader public, or did you know that the broader public had been aware of it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how much the word of these goals crept into general public awareness. It was certainly not uncommon in that time for substantial time to lag between the adoption of a decision or resolution and its publication in the Official Gazette, particularly for the Republika Srpska, the Bosnian Serb side. This was an unusually long period of time, and I think it's hard to believe that there was not some growth in public awareness of it over that year and a half, but the ultimate answer is: I don't know how much it became known in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask, Mr. Donia, during the discussion in the assembly, did the assembly resolve to keep it quiet and keep it just known by members of the assembly? Or when they discussed in the next two or three days, whether or not to publish it, was this information also passed on to the members of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the -- to my knowledge there was no discussion of that decision in the assembly. There was discussion among the top SDS leaders, Krajisnik, Koljevic and Karadzic, but not in -- it doesn't appear in the transcript of that session. So the discussion was a very closed one and a sort of small, small group of people who considered it. They -- obviously you had 50, 60 people at least who knew what the goals were and some of them were reflected very quickly in other meetings or discussions, so there clearly was some dissemination to other leaders of the Bosnian Serb movement, of the contents of the goals, and one can tell that because in some case they were articulated somewhat differently than they were in the actual session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So shall we then understand you to say, to be referring to about 60 people when you talked at page 12, line 13, "Immediately after the discussion in the assembly session," by referring to the assembly session you're referring to those 50 or 60 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thursday, 22nd of August, our trial, page 1504, line 1 through 16, this is what you say: [In English] "However, it is important, I think to look at the context in which a particular proposal was made and adopted and the way that people understood it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 1504 is what I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This page number is wrong because the transcript of that day starts with page 15486.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be transcript reference 15504 and that appears to begin at line 14, if that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I thank my colleague for helping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I meanwhile ask an additional question in relation to the public character of the six strategic goals, the matter was discussed during the 16th session of the -- of the assembly session. Was that a public session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was not. Thank you. And the transcript or the records of that session were not public either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were not made public at that time, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we've corrected the page reference and you said that the context was important. This is my question: Would you agree that in this report of yours about the assembly sessions, the sessions of the Republika Srpska, it is precisely context that is missing and it cannot be seen what events led to a particular discussion. Excerpts were taken from the debate itself at the sessions of the assembly of Republika Srpska. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- that's a couple of different questions. I would agree that my excerpts were taken from the debates themselves at the session. In answer to your question, Is it precisely context that is missing, I would say that's not completely the case. I attempted in the introduction to each section to provide some modest amount of context for the section that followed. And within the excerpts themselves there is a great deal of other information about the context, about the events that were taking place, about the specific vocabulary choices being made within the SDS and about the, I would say, flow of discussion within the time. So I wouldn't agree completely that this is without context completely. There is some there. I would have to say, looking at it today, I wish I had added more. The problem with that is, if you start introducing context into every session and explain the external circumstances, this gets to be a very long report and I really -- the idea behind this report was to let the Bosnian Serb leaders speak for themselves in their own words and then have the reader pursue further details, including what came before it and after it, and the specific event, context, separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I hope I have the right page finally, 15498, Thursday, the 22nd of August, line 6 to 10. This is the discussion you had with the Prosecutor. I'm going to read this out in English: [In English] "Q. And what consideration -- did you give additional consideration to the role of the accused in this particular case? "A. Yes. This report, which is similar to one that I prepared for earlier cases, was designed specifically to be tailored to the role and perceptions, as he expressed them, of the accused in this case." [Interpretation] It is precisely this report that is being referred to from the assembly of Republika Srpska. However, will you agree with me that in this report, it is not the words of General Mladic that were singled out but, rather, an enormous part of the report are not the words of General Mladic but of other persons, rather; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I would object to the phrasing of this question. The transcript reference from which this is drawn refer to the Sarajevo report. It may be a fine distinction, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are you willing to rephrase your question keeping in mind what Ms. Bibles said?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I might come back. I see that this paper which is very short is -- I don't know how it turned up to be a real mess. I will leave this to be checked during the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that we've come to page 35 in B/C/S or in English it is 37, page 37 of your report, about Sarajevo, P1999. I asked you because you say in the heading, itself, the simultaneous pursuit of Bosnian independence and Serb separatism. I asked you and I don't think I got an answer, when you say Bosnia, independence, Bosnian independence, is it true that this is actually the aspiration of two peoples from Bosnia-Herzegovina for independence, the Muslim and the Croat people, excluding the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think that's not a good characterisation of it. I would say that the principal nationalist political formations of the Bosnian Muslims and the Croats and individuals from those groups and from others, including Yugoslavs and Serbs, favoured independence or were sympathetic to it, were prepared to support it politically. The leading formation claiming to represent the Serb people, which is the SDS, was staunchly opposed to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to your research, how many Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina were in favour of independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Can you give us a percentage? Except for Mirko Pejanovic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't give you a number or percentage. I don't know that that is available, that there was any kind of public opinion survey that we would consider reliable that goes to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree, although you don't know the number and you don't know the percentage, that this was a negligible number of Serbs who would be in favour of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would not agree in the sense that it's very difficult to determine how many at that point were feeling that way, based on the evidence that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My colleague is helping me and he's saying what is your source, in terms of the Serbs voting in favour of independence, if we know that the vote was secret?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- that's a good question. I have to say I don't -- I don't recall seeing an official report of the electoral commission, for example, that gave that number. We certainly know that the political formations took the positions that they did, and the SDS urged Serbs to stay home. But what the percentages are, in terms of official reports, I can't recall seeing any official reports. There were many reports in the press about this at the time and some very precise numbers which were announced by the government, but I don't really know what the count, how the determination was made, if it was made at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Somebody is cooking something good. I don't know if you can feel the smell of food here in the courtroom as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's still some time before we go for lunch, Mr. Lukic, but the sooner you want to go for lunch, the more efficient your cross-examination would have to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that even before the war, at the time when this coalition government was in place, SDA/HDZ/SDS, the minister of foreign affairs of that joint government travelled in the east and asked that Bosnia-Herzegovina be admitted into the Islamic conference, the community of Islamic states?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's widely acknowledged to be the case by people who looked at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Military preparations in BH, 91-92, is the next heading. You're talking about the JNA in May 1992. This is page 39, and then on page 44, third paragraph in the English version, P1999, so could we please have this in e-court? Page 44 of this document in e-court, paragraph 3, in the B/C/S version, page 42, paragraph 2. You said: Confronted with a lack of manpower, the JNA tried to mobilise Bosnian Serbs for service in Croatia and ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot find this portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters have difficulties in finding the portion. Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is the last paragraph on that page, beginning with the words, "Faced with manpower."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 in English version, page 44, and paragraph 2 in B/C/S version on page 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your research, did you find that the JNA at the time, like before that, had an obligation according to the law to keep their units manned? That was in accordance with the constitution and the law and the internal regulations of the JNA as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not familiar enough with those internal regulations to know at what level that obligation existed. I would not think it was a constitutional obligation but, again, I don't -- I really don't know. It's clear that they were, that is the JNA senior officers, and for that matter Milosevic, were very determined to keep it manned and engaged in various strategies to try to keep it that way and to bring additional troops into the force in the fall of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask for a clarification. You said "additional troops," in addition to what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be in addition to the active serving troops. They mobilised reservists and found recruits from local Serb organisations in order to complete the -- continue the staffing. I mention in this report somewhere that in the fall of 1991, the -- I believe it was the Presidency endorsed the strategy of accepting volunteers into the JNA in addition to these other mobilisations of reservists that the senior command engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just before we take the break, the units were not manned at a level that was normal before that, before the Muslims and Croats left. The Serbs did not manage to have the units manned as they were before the departure of the Muslims and Croats. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- I'm a little bit confused about the question. The people who were trying to have the units manned as close to capacity as possible were not the Serbs particularly but JNA officers and, as I say, the senior political leadership of Yugoslavia at that time. So I'm not sure what your question pertains to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is: The level of manning of the units, was it normal, was it below the manning level, or above the manning level? Do you know? What we are suggesting is that it was below the prescribed level of manning.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For those units that I've had an opportunity to see numbers for, you would be right. They were below the maximum, below the authorised level in the cases that I've seen, and I rather think that's probably true of the army as it existed in its Croatian units anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. It's time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will take a break of 20 minutes. Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if it might be helpful in the examination for Dr. Donia to have a hard copy of his two reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there seems to be no problem looking at the body language of Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have it, if you don't mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I could print a clean copy with no highlights.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My copies have highlights too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Okay, clean copies will be provided to the witness. Mr. Donia, you may follow the usher. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you received a hard copy of your report about Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It will be easier for you. If we now move to page 43, paragraph 3 of your Sarajevo report. Now we are facing the same problem with regard to e-court. In e-court it should be 41, paragraph 3, and page 42 in B/C/S in e-court, paragraph 2. Are we on page 44 in English in e-court? Look at this portion where you speak about 28 September 1991, where you say that the JNA ordered reservists in BiH to active duty on 27th of September, 1991, and many Serb reservists and volunteers responded to the call and joined either the Croatian or BH. But the very next day, the Presidency of BH denounced the JNA's mobilisation order as illegal and thereby discouraging Muslims and Croats from joining the pro-Serbian JNA. Have you seen this Presidency's decision, ever?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. It's been a long time since I actually looked at it but it was published at the time and was very brief decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, Serb representatives were in the Presidency as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the decision that you saw, did you see that Serb representatives voted against such a decision of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you would agree that that was a time when even though there were joint organs such as the Presidency, all the decisions were taken by outvoting representatives of the Serb nation and against the interests of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree with either proposition that you make here. First of all, I don't think that all decisions were -- all decisions were taken by majority rule within the Presidency. But not all of them were a five-to-two vote at that time. There were a few decisions as I recall that people agreed on, and I don't -- you know, against the interests of the Serb people, I would say against the interests as interpreted by the SDS leaders and Serb representatives on the Presidency at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In order to demonstrate whether that was solely the interests of SDS representatives but also the Serbian people as a whole, a plebiscite was called - is that right - and in this plebiscite the Serbs voted, if not 100 per cent, but nearly 100 per cent, against the succession of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Neither part of your proposition here is correct. First of all, the referendum, or, I'm sorry, the plebiscite was not called in response to this decision. It was called in response to the developments after the 15th of October, when the SDS leadership had begun taking these -- the steps toward a separate Serb state. And the proposition that was voted upon was not -- did not pertain, did not say anything about the Serb, as I recall, it didn't say anything about the independence. It simply said that if you voted yes, you wanted to remain in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it is the way in which you phrase it. I wondered over the last few questions, you put your questions in such a way that it elicits contradiction by the expert whereas to the substance, I think you could even have agreed on the matter, that is that at the time collegial decisions were sometimes or perhaps even often that it was an opportunity to outvote a minority. I think the Prosecution most likely would not disagree with that. Second, that the Serb leaders voted in what they thought to be in the best interests of Serbs, might not have found any opposition either. Now, here for the same, that there was a referendum in which Serbs could express themselves on whether they wanted to stay within Yugoslavia, yes or no, there may be no dispute about that either. It is the way in which the questions are phrased by you enter into a debate whereas from what I understand on the basic matters, I would not expect the Prosecution to disagree, but I am also looking at Ms. Bibles whether my assumption is a fair one.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So why not focus on what basically is what you want to draw our attention to? That outvoting was -- happened, and that the decisions may not have been agreed by the Serb leaders because they thought them not to be in the best interests of Serbian citizens? That's what you want to establish, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it's pretty differently explained in this report so that's why I have to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The report doesn't say anything about it. The report here underlines we are looking at at this moment just gives facts, the very next day, no dispute about whether it was the next day or any other time, the Presidency of the BiH, and you want to tell us that that is not necessarily unanimous. I think there is no -- might be no disagreement, denounced the JNA's mobilisation order as illegal, there may be no dispute about that either, thereby discouraging Muslim and Croats reservists in BiH from joining the Serb-leaning JNA. There is nothing in it there which suggested that it was unanimous, that it was suggested that it was in the best interests of Serbs. Not in any way. So you're fighting against something which isn't there. And you want to draw our attention to specific aspects, not necessarily unanimous, perhaps outvoted and therefore perhaps not having considered sufficiently the interests of the Serbs, that is, I would say, not very difficult most likely to agree upon, and the way in which you phrased the questions elicits minor disputes about the language rather than on the substance. But I'm also looking at you at this moment, Mr. Donia, whether you would agree with my analysis that on the basic matters, you agree with Mr. Lukic but it's mainly the way in which he phrases the questions that causes you to contradict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's very inefficient. It doesn't bring you where you want to be, Mr. Lukic, and it's easily good to get there in approximately 20, 25, 30 per cent of the time you're using. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, is it true that in your report, what you're trying to say is that it was the Serbs who were actively involved and that it was the Serbs who were striving for the break-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I stated that previously that this was -- there were two tracks that were being simultaneously pursued, one by the SDS Serb side moving towards separatism and the other moving toward independence on the part of the Croat and Muslim leadership. So I think your statement is correct but that's only part of what I'm trying to point out. These two things were happening. They were interactive and they were proceeding along very different paths but at about the same time and pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I must say that it's difficult for me to understand, therefore I am a bit perplexed by the comment of Judge Orie. At the time when Yugoslavia was in existence, and when the Serbs wanted the existing state of Yugoslavia to remain there, for them to be qualified and described as separatists, I can't understand that. How is it possible for someone who wants to remain living in the existing state can be described as a separatist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you answer the question, Mr. Donia, could I ask the following question, and perhaps you'll answer the two of them together: Is it true that the strife for separating Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia caused the Serbs who had been in favour of staying within Yugoslavia even more to separate themselves from the Croat and Bosnians in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it intensified their desire to do that, yes. There was some desire to do so before the events of the 15th of October, but it certainly intensified their wish to move forward with these separatist activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, as far as Mr. Lukic's question is concerned, do I understand that you disagree with him that the Serbs wanted to stay together with the Croats and the Muslims in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would have been their first preference, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would have been their first preference, together, to stay with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All of them within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And, in fact, they worked to that end substantially prior to the events of mid-October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where you say "I think it intensified their desire to do that," that was their wish to remain or their wish to separate from the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wished to separate from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Already before the mid-October events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I think as I say, that was not -- that was not their first preference at that point. They had kind of a primary objective and a backup objective. Primary objective was to keep Bosnia, all of it and everyone in it, in Yugoslavia. That's what they first and foremost sought. Their secondary -- their fall back position was to separate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was intensified after the 15th of October.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was, and my argument would be that the events of the 15th basically ended any realistic hope of the primary objective being achieved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you have any follow-up questions please put them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, I'm sorry for this short pause because I had to consult with my colleague. Is it, in fact, true that the Bosnian Serbs did not want secession but, rather they said this: We want the whole of Bosnia to remain within Yugoslavia, but if the Croat and Muslim peoples do not want that, then we, ourselves, would wish to remain in Yugoslavia and we are willing to let them go away? Was that actually the position of the Serbian leadership in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was indeed the position of the Bosnian Serb leadership, and in fact follows almost word for word the description that I've given of General Kadijevic's view within the JNA, which I think starts on page -- this quote that starts on page 41. That was the position. At the same time that they took the position that they wanted no change in the status quo, only to remain in Yugoslavia, they intensified their separatist activities citing as the justification the referendum, the plebiscite that was held. In other words, they used the statement of just simply, "I want to stay" to justify things beyond which, beyond what that proposition actually stated. So I think both are correct. That was their position. That was their official position. And they stood by it firmly and at the same time began organising separatist activities. I mentioned this interesting exchange from an assembly session yesterday in which one of the delegates stood up and said, Wait a minute, I thought we were for staying in Yugoslavia. And if that's true, we shouldn't need to do anything. We are already in Yugoslavia. And the leadership of course responded that that's not enough. We have to pursue these separatist activities in order to break away from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at the time, a declaration was issued, adopted by Serb representatives, and that everything contained therein was conditional? Nothing was defined definitely. If the other side does this we shall do that? If the other side does that, we shall do this? Up until that time, we are not going to make any moves. Is that actually the position of the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was their official position, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 43 of your report, which is 45 in e-court, last paragraph, 43 in e-court in B/C/S, they -- since --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we just be given a second to find the paragraph? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the interpreters are asking for a moment to find the relevant portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if you slowly proceed now. And indicate from where you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know it's the last paragraph in English and -- it's this separate paragraph, which reads: "When it proved fruitless for the JNA to orient the Muslim part of Bosnia's leadership towards a new Yugoslav state made of those Yugoslav nations who still wanted it, we had to orient ourselves towards concrete co-operation with the representatives of the Serb nation and with the Serb people as a whole, never closing the door on co-operation with others, individuals who supported a new Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you know about these negotiations that were going on about -- and about the offers made by the JNA to all the peoples, i.e., Muslims, Croats and others in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the negotiations that you are making reference to? What was the source of what you're citing here, what kind of negotiations were in question, and what offers were made by the JNA? Do you know anything at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quoting here General Kadijevic, and quoting him for the purpose of explaining the motivation and procedures that were part of this reorientation of the JNA to -- reorientation to the Serb people and what he viewed as Serb interests. I don't see any reference to negotiations in the quote anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Shall we read the first sentence again which reads: "When it proved fruitless for the JNA to orient the Muslim part of Bosnia's leadership toward a new Yugoslav state made of those Yugoslav nations who really wanted it." But it's all right if you're unable to talk about this, then I'm going to ask you something about a broader context. At the time, were you aware that Alija Izetbegovic was offered to be the first prime minister of the Yugoslavia that would include Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia and Montenegro? I even believe that Macedonia featured in these talks as well.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm aware of a meeting that Adil Zulfikarpasic had with Milosevic which was I think in June or July in which he made an almost implausibly generous offer to restructure Yugoslavia and its succession process in such a way that the SDA could select the first president or Bosnia could select the first president of the federal Presidency, and also agreed to name a number of Muslim JNA officers to key positions in the army. That's -- I think, as I recall, that was in June, maybe early July. But that's not quite the same thing that you're talking about and I don't frankly know of any negotiations in the period we are talking about here, which I take to be the time of the failed mobilisations or the bifurcation of the mobilisations which is in September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you're referring to June, July, you're talking about 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we saw that mobilisation was announced and that a decision on the Presidency was adopted by outvoting, that Muslims and Croats failed to respond to the call-up. Then we come, as you say, to mid-October when Serbs indicated their efforts to separate themselves from Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm going to say to you that the Defence case was that the Serbs only wanted to remain in the same state with everybody else, if possible, and if that was not plausible, then to remain with those who wanted to stay and let the others go. I asked you about the plebiscite and now my colleague has provided some information about that. I'm asking you do you know that the plebiscite of the Serbian people took place on the 9th and 10th November 1991 when 1.350.000 citizens or 96.4 per cent of citizens voted for an independent state that could either be an independent one or part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before the witness answers, you referred to 96 per cent of the citizens, citizens of what state?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everybody was invited to vote in the plebiscite. However, this plebiscite organised by the SDS almost only Serbs turned out, the number of Muslims and Croats who turned up was negligible. The referendum held on the 29th February 1992 and 1st March 1992 was held by -- with participation of the majority of Muslims and Croats and the negligible number of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm coming to assist my colleague. 96.4 per cent of citizens. You were asked for an explanation. May I take it that you wanted to say 96.4 per cent of the citizens that participated in the vote voted for?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the simple answer. You come with a long explanation on matters not asked for. But apparently my suggestion for the answer seems to satisfy my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for being vague and not precise enough. That's the concise answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's very important to be concise when you ask questions, Mr. Lukic, and when we ask for clarification it's also equally important to listen to the question and answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 46 of your report, in the English version, in e-court, that is, or rather page 44 of your report itself, in the second paragraph, on page 44, paragraph 1 of the B/C/S version, you say, in an article that was published, let us just wait for a moment. There is a reference to the 22nd of November, 1991. So it's easy to find. In an article published on the 22nd of November, 1991, in the Sarajevo magazine "Slobodan Bosna" a journalist claimed to have documents showing that the SDS had formed a war staff and made detailed plans to besiege and attack Sarajevo in the event of a war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the text of the report reads, "Journalists claimed" not a journalist claimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have translation on B/C/S. I cut it out. If it's in English I would accept English version of course, but in B/C/S it's "jedan novinar je tvrdiu," [Interpretation] "a journalist claimed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. In English it says "journalists." In English it's then a translation error. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doesn't affect my question anyway. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You used "Slobodna Bosna," a newspaper, here as a source for your report, and in footnote 118 that you refer to here, as a source, we see that the title of that text is, "Sarajevo as a Chetnik target." Would you agree at the time Chetnik was a pejorative name for Serbs that was used in the Muslim press?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was used in not only the Muslim -- I would say -- it's a pro-Muslim publications but Croat and other publications and it definitely was a pejorative. Not clear sometimes whether it was referring just to armed Serbs or all Serbs but it was certainly widely used.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us be specific. Widely used by who? By the Muslims and Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, could I, in response to the earlier exchange, there was a question that was asked of me which I didn't get to answer, as you addressed some remarks to Mr. Lukic. And it pertained to the content of the plebiscite of the 9th and 10th of November, and I believe the representation was, Mr. Lukic, that the plebiscite gave voters a choice of whether to stay in Yugoslavia or become part of a separate state. That is not my recollection of the content of the wording of the resolution on which voters voted. My recollection is that it only asked if voters wanted to remain in Yugoslavia and had no further reference to independence or even a separate Serb state. It simply pertained to independence and perhaps some of the regional associations that were being formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This document that we discussed and that footnote 118 of your paper refers to, that is mentioned in "Slobodna Bosna," did you see that? Did you see that document that they say exists, namely that a war staff was established and there is a plan for a war siege of Sarajevo? I'm not referring to the article itself. I'm referring to the document that the article refers to.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen that document, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Slobodna Bosna," we will agree, won't we, is a paper that exclusively represented the views and positions of the representatives of the Muslim people; isn't that right? At that time and even today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree that that's quite right. I think it was founded as a -- first of all, as a weekly. It wasn't really a newspaper, and it specialised in muckraking, aggressive investigative journalism. It was certainly oriented in that time principally to the needs or interests of the Muslim leadership, but also at times became very critical of developments within the SDA and published some of those items too, but its principal orientation I would agree was, as you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you would have avoided the word "exclusively" in your question and if you would have phrased the question that whether it principally reflected that, then you would have had exactly the same answer in approximately a split of the time you used now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but then that would be my position and my position that they exclusively, exclusively, wrote by conveying the positions of the Muslim leadership. They would criticise even a politician who would be in a different faction, again only representing the interests of the politicians who represented the Muslim people. So that is my position. If Dr. Donia corrects me, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I accept that if you think it's exclusively, how unlikely that might be, if that's your position, then you should ask for that rather than to move immediately to it being mainly reflecting the interests, then of course you're free to do so. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to go to page 48 in e-court, in the English version, we need paragraph 4. In B/C/S it's page 46, and that is the 46th version of your paper in the English language.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what was the page number in the English paper copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 4. It starts, "Although he successfully kept most ..." it's paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is page 44 in the English version of the report itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It moved. It was two pages different, but thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the text is as follows: "Although he successfully kept most JNA resources from Croat and Bosnian government forces Kukanjac was unable to arrange the JNA's peaceful withdrawal from its urban barracks. Some JNA facilities had been under either surveillance or actual blockade by government forces since early 1992." When you say government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at that time, there were still Serbs in that government; right? January, February 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, there were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree actually that the forces that besieged the facilities of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were not loyal to the government of the BH but actually loyal to the SDA, the party of Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time, it's kind of difficult to tell exactly who was doing what. I think as a general statement, you can say they were loyal to the SDA or its programme, and that's why they were participating in the besieging or surrounding of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You would agree that you did not mean that they were loyal to Biljana Plavsic or Nikola Koljevic who at the time were the Serb representatives in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they had really no personal loyalty to either of those persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, this same paragraph, you say: "Most problematic were huge barracks in Tuzla and north-eastern Bosnia, the sprawling Marsal Tito barracks on the near west side of Sarajevo and the century-old headquarters of the second military group on the south side of the Miljacka river in Sarajevo. Of those three facilities, only the Tito barracks were evacuated peacefully. And that only a month after Kukanjac left his command. In the other two cases locally negotiated agreements broke down and the withdrawing JNA columns were attacked by forces of or loyal to the Bosnian government." At this time, the BH government had no Serb representatives any longer when the barracks were attacked; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say -- I believe that's correct. I think those seats, those seats were vacant, the two seats on the Presidency, as of the 6th of April and were not filled again until, I believe, sometime in early June. So you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But when you say "manned," you mean co-opting Mirko Pejanovic and that is what Alija Izetbegovic did, it's not that new elections were held in which the Serb people would elect their new representatives into the government?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that's your position and your firm conviction but the -- there actually were two members put in -- appointed to the position to represent Serbs in Bosnia. One was Pejanovic and the other was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Kecmanovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kecmanovic. Who subsequently did not stay in Sarajevo, but for a period of time the two of them as the, I believe, next two vote getters from the 1990 elections were put in those positions by the Presidency appointing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Pejanovic was a representative of the Communist Party; isn't that right? And he won 15 per cent of the vote. So maybe Croats and Muslims and Serbs voted for him. It's not that he was a representative of a Serb national party; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not the case. He, first of all, was the candidate of the reformed Socialist Alliance, not the League of Communists, and that party in its new name, I believe, was the Democratic Socialist Party. And he was, as I say, third or fourth among Serb vote getters in this very complex arrangement which didn't even send the top seven people to the Presidency. It sent the top two vote getters in each of the three national categories and then one in the category of others. So it wasn't the practice, it's very unlikely that anyone other than Serbs voted for him, not because of the way that the thing was structured but because the parties all urged people only to vote for members of their own ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you the following: When you refer to government or loyal to government forces, did you intend to say loyal to all the individual members of the government or forces loyal to all the individual members of that government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I meant to -- loyal to the majority, to the body itself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, all your questions are focused on reading in the report something which isn't there and then to challenge that. If it says "government," the Chamber understands this as what the government by majority and any other way had decided to do or not to do. Again, you are challenging things which seems not to be in the document, and are suggesting a meaning of the report which is not there, if I understand Mr. Donia well. And that's a rather useless exercise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now that you say that it's not in the report, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think Mr. Mladic is seeking your attention or he's thinking about the break. I think we would have a break in five minutes from now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The report says that these reports were loyal to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In your view, then, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did it issue orders to these forces that surrounded the barracks and facilities of the JNA from the beginning of the year?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen them, looked at them. I'm confident it did. The Presidency issued orders to military leaders who at that time would have been the TO. You're dating this from the beginning of the year. The actual siege of the barracks surrounding and cutting them off really didn't happen, wasn't completed, until May, particularly starting about May 2nd of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know, then, whether the representatives of the Serb people in that government were informed of such orders, or were these orders issued behind their backs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say here in this last passage that we read out that in the other two cases, local agreements were not observed and withdrawing JNA columns were attacked by forces who were loyal to the Bosnian government. Who was it that did not observe locally negotiated agreements, the JNA that was withdrawing or forces loyal to the BH at the time, those who were attacking the columns?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, each side claimed that the other was not respecting the agreement. For example, in Tuzla, the Tuzla city government accused the JNA of withdrawing its weapons and ammunition with the column, in violation of the agreement that they had reached. In that same situation, the JNA accused the Tuzla local forces of attacking the column unprovoked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the course of your work, did you learn that the JNA did not respect something that had been agreed or is this a shameless lie that was just used to justify attacks against a column that did not offer any resistance whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There certainly is evidence that the -- in the case of the Tuzla column, that the JNA was withdrawing substantial weapons and ammunition. One of the trucks that was attacked clearly was carrying ammunition because it exploded during the fire-fight and burned for a couple of hours, throwing flames several hundred feet in the air. So it seems to me there is some evidence that the JNA was indeed withdrawing weapons and ammunition, in that case at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony then, that in your research you came across information to the effect that the JNA soldiers were supposed to withdraw unarmed or did the agreement precisely provide for them withdrawing with their weapons?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't believe -- there was, I think part of the agreement in the case of the Sarajevo withdrawal from the 2nd Army headquarters, was that the withdrawing troops could have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just stop you for a moment? We were in Tuzla, weren't we, Mr. Lukic? The answer now moves to Sarajevo. Could we first check whether you have any knowledge about what exactly was agreed upon, if we are talking about local agreement, in Tuzla, as far as taking your arms with you when withdrawing? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've actually looked at that pretty closely and I don't see any -- I don't know of any provision in the agreement as it was finally reached for them to withdraw with their arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But also not to withdraw without their arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That that was, as I understand it, that was the final agreement. Now, it was only a verbal agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. You say as you understand it, that is your understanding is then that they would withdraw unarmed or without their arms, which is not exactly the same, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, without their weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Without their weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was my understanding of the second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of an oral agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two agreements and one fell apart immediately and the other actually was what allowed the column to begin its exit and then the fire-fight broke out at that point. And it was the second verbal agreement that in speaking to the people who were party to it, they said that there was no stipulation that they could take their weapons with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, but that's -- was there any stipulation that they could not take their weapons with them? Were they prohibited from doing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's my understanding, that they were prohibited from doing that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Explicitly or implicit by not having a stipulation that they could take their weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I frankly don't know enough because it was a verbal agreement and people I talked to couldn't recall exactly what the substance of it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Having dealt with Tuzla, I don't know, Mr. Lukic, whether you want to proceed anything further in relation to Sarajevo but perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One minute with Tuzla and then we can go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say a conflict broke out. In that conflict, how many casualties were there on the other side, that is to say not the JNA, on this other side that attacked the column, there weren't any casualties; right? There was no conflict there. This was an attack against children sitting on trucks and that were killed and burned, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know of attacks against children in this -- in this process. It --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They were 19 or 18 years old; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In uniform, I think that's, you know, not -- not the definition of a child here. Look, there was -- again, this has been litigated actually in a Belgrade court for a long time, without, in my view, reaching any conclusion about who began this action, and exactly, you know, what -- what caused the outbreak of violence, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Could you please tell us before the break, these soldiers from the column, how many people did they kill on the Muslim side? How many Muslims were killed then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I could tell you the number of casualties that were counted in the column. The Bosnian side counted 34. Milosevic in his -- one of his testimonies submitted the number 47. I think that's a range within which the number of people killed in the column could be placed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one additional question, then? Do you not know the number of casualties among the Muslims, or do you say, I never heard about any casualties among the Muslims during this violence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say the latter. I have not heard, do not know of any casualties, on the Tuzla government side of the thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic? That's it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break and we resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. There was one issue remaining from this morning. I think I instructed the Registry to attach the translation to P1987. I do understand that it was MFI'd for the lack of a translation. Hereby, the Chamber decides that P1987 is admitted into evidence. Apart from that, the Chamber was informed that the Registry had followed up on all the instructions that the Chamber issued this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, now I would focus on your report which is called, "Siege." It's page 54 in e-court, it should be 50 in your report. And in B/C/S it should be page 51. In one of the previous parts of your report, you said that there was a reorganisation of Sarajevo by encouraging the Serbs to leave the Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic please repeat slowly the rest of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat slowly the rest of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "And to eliminate the presence of the majority of Serbs from the territory under their control." That was a quotation. Is it true that people left Bosnia-Herzegovina in fear; that they left the territory under the control of the other side for that reason?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know -- I don't see where I wrote this statement or made this statement, to eliminate the presence of a majority of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, you say that this was the Serbian strategy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, where do we find it? That's the first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to speed up but it's English page 52 in e-court. And it's B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should be 48 in the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed, just under the heading, "Establishing the siege," that first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And 49 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
