utterances.text: The title is, "Establishing the siege," and you say that a democrat -- demographic reordering of Sarajevo by urging Serbs to leave Sarajevo and eliminating the presence of most non-Serbs on territory they controlled. Yesterday, you told us that the Serbs who wanted to leave Sarajevo after the 2nd of May were no longer able to do that. And my question was, is it true that all the peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina were leaving the territory controlled by the other side for the reasons of fear?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you've again summarised something I said yesterday and I didn't say that. I didn't say that Serbs who wanted to leave Sarajevo after the 2nd of May were no longer able to do that. I said that there were some barriers imposed to their departure but that it appeared to me that no one who wanted to get out was not able to get out. So to turn to your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let us continue from here. According to your knowledge, who of the Serbs managed to leave the Sarajevo? How many of them and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we suggest that you look at that paragraph in this "Establishing the siege" carefully because I'm not quite sure that your question is in line with the statement that is made there. Eliminating the presence of most non-Serbs is what the statement says, not Serbs, if you look at the report itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it says that the Serbs were encouraged to leave Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, in order to eliminate non-Serbs. Or ask the author. Here he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the witness returned to previous answer from yesterday telling that I quoted him wrongly and I just wanted clarification from the witness now to give us examples, numbers, sources, how he learned who from the Serb people left Sarajevo. I will come back to that second part of elimination, and that was my question, wasn't that true that every nation in Bosnia left the territory that is not under control of its own army. And I haven't got the response yet. I will come back to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You will come back to it but you're mixing it with what is already here and I don't think -- but, look, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us any examples, any numbers of how many Serbs managed to leave Sarajevo and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the number of Serbs in Sarajevo, according to the 1991 census, was something around 150.000. And I think some of those, there was an initial wave of departures just in the beginning weeks of the armed conflict, but most actually stayed at that time, and then a good number of those actually departed in the course of the spring and summer of 1992, and subsequently in the war. So that the estimates of numbers of Serbs who remained in Sarajevo at the time the siege ended, which was in February of 1996, ranges from a high of maybe 60.000 to as little as 20.000. Now, those are not census figures but they are estimates by various people who -- mainly estimates by Serbs who stayed in Sarajevo during the war. So it's clear that those people who wanted to get out were able to get out, although, as I say, often not without some difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you believe that when we question Sarajevo Serbs, that they are going to corroborate the statement that you have just made that anyone who wanted to leave was free to go?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you've mischaracterised my testimony. I said that they were able to get out but not without in some cases substantial difficulty. And I do expect, if you talk to a representative number of people, to be borne out on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you wouldn't agree with the Defence case that Serbs were unable to get out of Sarajevo because they were held there not only as a human shield but they were also used for digging trenches, that money was being extorted from them and that they were summarily executed without any guilt? Would you agree that this is the characterisation of Sarajevo situation in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it's a caricature, propagandistic caricature of the situation in Sarajevo, not an accurate characterisation of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek clarification. Is it your position, Mr. Lukic, that all of the Serbs were either held as a human shield, used for digging trenches or that those instances occurred? Because we are talking about the Serbs, the Serbs not being able to leave, the Serbs. Is it your position that all of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not all, of course it's very hard to say all. We have Mirko Pejanovic who was enjoying that period of time living in Sarajevo of course, and a few like him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is it your position that none of the Serbs managed to get out and do you have any numbers so because I'm troubled by the Serbs, Serbs, majorities. Do we have -- what is the position of the Defence on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only few Serbs were able to leave Sarajevo, only they were loaded with money, if they were able to pay a lot of money for their departure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- the position is clear now. Could you comment then on these statements, that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's not the case. Many of those Serbs who stayed were, in fact, people who stayed because they had jobs, their roots were in the community. One prominent Serb who stayed, Dane Olbina, wrote in his diary that we will share the destiny of this city. That was his reason for staying. And I think people had various reasons for staying, as well as various reasons for living -- or for leaving, those who did, but I disagree with this characterised description of everyone being persecuted and unable to leave. That's simply not the case. The vast majority of Serbs who lived in Sarajevo as of the first day of siege left, something like 60, 70 per cent of them left the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But could you express that in numbers more or less?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I say, 150.000, sometimes Serb SDS and Serb leaders wanted to include Yugoslavs in that number and get it up to 200.000 but I would accept the census number, from something around 150.000 down to something between, let's say 20- and 60.000 at the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means 100.000 left approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Such instances, digging trenches, being held as -- did such instances happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did, and they happened principally in the first several months of the war, and they were principally done by these paramilitaries or gangs before they were really brought under control by the government but they certainly did take place. There were also others, non-Serbs, who were forced to dig trenches, so it's not specifically, not solely a matter of ethnicity but, yes, there were such cases, to be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you quantify those instances? If even only approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just -- very difficult to do. Maybe, I don't know, 20-, 30.000 may have been involved, let's say of all citizens of Sarajevo may have been involved in some form of forced labour, whether short or longer period of time, in the course of the siege.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is still a considerable number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 150.000 Serbs, that involves the whole Sarajevo including the parts under the Serb control, or was someone not included in that number?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that number which was used by Karadzic and General Mladic for that matter was derived from the 1991 census which included all ten municipalities of Sarajevo that were as it existed from 1977 on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you whether you can quantify those Serbs who lived in an area where they didn't have to move in order to be or rather to remain under Serb control? Would that be, for example, people in Pale wouldn't have to move, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. That was certainly true in a couple of these municipalities, very -- not so in the western part of the city where really there was a Serb takeover that was in many cases violent. It's hard to quantify. I would guess that if you take -- I mean, Pale, some of these areas were not that heavily populated generally so perhaps, I don't know, I'd say 40- to 50.000 maybe Serbs lived in 1991 in areas that were controlled by Serb forces after, let's say, May 2, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which therefore reduces the number of 150.000 to 100.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And those that had left to roughly 50- to 60.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which is a different number from the one you gave me a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm trying to reconcile the 1991 census figure with what we really saw at the end of the conflict in February of 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The post war situation was supposedly better than the one during the war. Do you have any information how many Serbs are living in Sarajevo nowadays expressed either percentage wise or in numbers? And I'm talking about the part which is within the Federation today.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I really have no idea. That's far beyond the scope of what I've attempted to address here and don't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that only a handful of Serbs and Croats are living in Sarajevo nowadays?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just -- no. I don't -- I don't think it's just a handful. I don't know how many you mean by a handful but we -- I don't think -- simply don't know that. There was a kind of enumeration from 2002 that was made in Sarajevo only, I believe, and I just don't have those numbers at hand. I would not agree with your statement that it was necessarily better after the war. I think it probably -- certainly the number declined in areas within the Federation. But, remember, there was a large shift of boundaries in 1996 to correspond to the lines that were drawn in the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as Sarajevo is concerned, the part that was given to the Federation was bigger than the one that was under the BH Army control during the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- yes, it was as I mentioned I believe in the report, something like 59 per cent of the pre-war ten municipalities and during the war the area was considerably constricted from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is invited to remain seated and even instructed to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please keep the volume down. Please keep the volume down. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, is it true that the SDA had started taking over departments of the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo and thus they acquired full control under public security stations of Stari Grad, Centar, Novo Sarajevo and Novi Grad, which was, in fact, something that constitutes the major part of Sarajevo downtown?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say at the time, what time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The time that you included in the title outline of the siege. That is to say when things started developing before the outbreak of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were SDA-backed efforts to -- successful efforts, to take control of public security stations that were often in conflict with those being engaged in by the SDS. So it was kind of a two-party process, in some cases even three-party process in which both the SDA and the government on the one hand and the SDS on the other tried to seize police stations and order the obedience of policemen within each of the stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 56 in e-court, third paragraph, and 53, third paragraph, in B/C/S, and 56 in English, probably 49 in your report, you say that General Mladic, the appointed commander of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic please read slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, first of all, page 56 in e-court would correspond with page 52 in the English hard copy. I think there is a -- usually a difference of four pages, already for a long time, and could you please slowly read what you want to refer to. And I take it you are reading from the middle of the page: "General Mladic, the newly designated commander of the VRS urged that heavy weapons be placed strategically around the city." That's where you started reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please continue whatever you want to read further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't mean to read further. If you want I can read further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I don't. I just started reading where you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, there existed in the city of Sarajevo numerous units, as you call them, loyal to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you find out from the sources the number of heavy weaponry in the city of Sarajevo that later became the position -- possession of the 1st Corps of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your work, did you find out how many offensives were launched from the city of Sarajevo against the Serbian positions during the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have described several of them in the course of the report, which, as you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know the total number of offensives?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- didn't count the total number of offensives just like I didn't count the total number of gun barrels on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Fair enough. [Interpretation] Do you know that the Muslim politicians and military commanders refused to accept demilitarisation of the city that had been offered by the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure specifically what you're referring to. I don't -- don't know, sitting here, that -- of situations in which they discussed but then rejected that. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your research, did you acquire information that the Serbian side constantly proposed a permanent cease of hostilities that were rejected by the Muslim side and that they only agreed to intermittent cease of hostilities? Did you study any UN documents on that topic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you can see in the report, I've made some study of UN documents over the course of the war pertaining to negotiations. I wouldn't accept that -- agree with that characterisation of the negotiations as a whole. I think there was much more give and take, back and forth than that, than you've described here. I think that it's fair to say that there was more readiness on the Serb side to declare a cessation of hostilities once they had completed their conquest of about 70 per cent of Bosnia and in fact they declared an end to the war in December of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. You speak about controlling a compact and interlinked territory in your report. It's page 60 in e-court, paragraph 2. B/C/S version 56, paragraph 2. I suppose this is also 56th page of your report. You are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are talking about meeting in Graz, when Mr. Karadzic on 6 May 1992 met with Mate Boban, and you say Croatian nationalist leader. Later on, the European Community did not accept these agreements. This is on 61 page in e-court. Next page, paragraph second, page 56 of the B/C/S, once they learned that the Muslim side did not participate in these negotiations and did not express their views. Would you agree that the European Community did not react in the equal manner when a referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was held? In other words, they were not interested in what the third side, that is to say the Serbs, had to say about it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't agree at all. You've kind of mixed two time periods which were very different in character, but if you go back to the earlier time period that you're speaking about, in fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the beginning of March and beginning of May, so there is a two month difference; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before we continue on this matter, is it your intention to put on an equal level an agreement agreed upon or not agreed upon by certain parties to the outcome of an election or a referendum? Is that what you intend to do, to say, Well, since you did not recognise the vote of the Serbs, therefore that's inequal treatment where you do not accept an agreement binding a party which never took part in the negotiations or the agreement? Is that what you want to compare? If that's the case, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to show the double standards that the European community had, and the representatives of the Serb people and representatives of Serb parties were aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I do understand that you want to show the double standards. My question was, however, a different one is whether not being a party and not having agreed upon something, is that the same as having lost an election or is that comparable? That was my question, whether you intended to compare the two as equal. Apart from what you then wanted to establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're talking about referendum now, when you say lost the election. Referendum was illegally conducted and results of the referendum are illegal and unconstitutional since you have to have three-quarters of votes to change the constitution. And that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you really wanted to compare the outcome as being --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of an equal --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not the election, the referendum without the Serbian people according to the constitution would not be legal and it was illegal but the EU at that time did not want to look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear to me you want to compare the two as being equal for analytical purposes. Would you please, then, answer the question? I think I interrupted you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you think that there were double standards in the EU, and the EU was on the side that wanted to destroy Yugoslavia openly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And specifically, the Badinter Commission of the European Community in its decision regarding Bosnia-Herzegovina in January of 1992 specifically took note of the Serb plebiscite, and treated that as an expression of the Serb people of Bosnia-Herzegovina that they were opposed to independence, and it was then on that basis that the EC invited Bosnia-Herzegovina to conduct a referendum on the basis -- without regard to differentiation by ethnicity on the question of independence, and short of that being done, the EC was not prepared to move forward to recognise the independence of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The outcome was known, wasn't it? It was known that there would be a majority vote, that the Serbs would be outvoted, as they were in the Presidency, as they were in the assembly, and that is why we had an instrument called constituent peoples whereby it was prohibited to have one particular people outvoted. Although you're not an expert in constitutional law, you knew that at the time there was this principle of constituent peoples which prohibited one constituent people in Bosnia-Herzegovina being outvoted by the other two. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try to unsort this. First the question was the outcome known? I think there were some in the EC who assumed that they knew what the result would be. But the fact is that in relatively last minute, the HDZ wavered in its support for independence, and objected to the specific language of the referendum, and only after some consideration decided to go ahead and actually support a vote in favour of independence. So I have to question whether they really knew or even thought, had great conviction, of the outcome. They were, after all, in the process of trying to impose some order on this whole business of parts of Yugoslavia and the Soviet Union becoming independent. That was their orientation. That was the task of the Badinter Commission. So was the result foreknown? I really don't think so. And even if it was, they wanted to establish the principle of majority vote. They had no interest in the -- they really did not recognise this principle of constituent nations, which was, after all, rooted in a Stalinist time in understanding of nationality polity in the Soviet Union. In addition, the principle of constituent nations really didn't apply in the Presidency, was clearly established, I believe, in the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it did not apply in any code that I know of to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Presidency does not pass laws and cannot change the constitution. They pass decrees and that is why it didn't pertain to them. However, we are going to move from this subject of constituency. We are going to elaborate on that with someone else. Thank you for your effort to try to help us. Reading UN documents, did you come across any traces to the effect that Muslim politicians were preventing supplies from reaching the city, the repair of electricity, gas, water, in order to portray the situation in town worse than it actually was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also knew of the existence of the airport -- or, rather, a tunnel underneath the airport. We see that from the paper. When we now discussed the possibility for Serbs to leave town, I should ask you the following. Actually, you knew and you mentioned that also, that through this tunnel, units were being brought in and taken out of Sarajevo through this tunnel. Did you ever come across information to the effect that anyone who was of Serb ethnicity could leave through that tunnel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think the tunnel was open to anyone of any ethnicity just to freely leave. It was primarily built for military purposes, the passage of food and humanitarian aid, and military personnel, rather than civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You saw through your work that Muslim authorities actually did give permits for entering and leaving through that tunnel; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen any of those. Certainly wouldn't doubt that they were issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know of armed clashes within Sarajevo between different Muslim formations, in 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such, yes. There were a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the attitude of the HVO towards the Army of BH in Sarajevo? What was the attitude of the HVO headquarters in Kiseljak? Did they help or not help the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did they contribute to them or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's several questions. I think the answer depends on what time period you're speaking of. At the beginning of the conflict, the HVO in general was allied with the ARBiH. There was considerable tension between them, as there was politically between the political leaderships, but there were plenty of HVO units in Sarajevo co-operating with the ARBiH in the defence of the city. That certainly changed after the outbreak of war in Central Bosnia between the HVO and the ARBiH, which really started in let's say in October of 1992 but became much more widespread in spring of 1993. And at that point, most of those units left Sarajevo or at least focused their activities only on the area of Stup and a couple of other Croat-inhabited areas and of course eventually the co-operation between them broke down completely. And I think the -- I can't really address specifically what the headquarters in Kiseljak did. I certainly know that the HVO entered into broad co-operative arrangements with the VRS and traded a lot of materiel over that line, but it also co-operated at times with the ARBiH even in the circumstances of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the HVO contributed through most of the war to the blockade of the Muslim forces within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say part of the war, and, again, that's a kind of question that calls for breaking down specific time periods. Probably more than the other two sides the HVO was in a position to play an opportunistic role and so at times did, indeed, enforce the blockade; at other times, did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for elevations surrounding Sarajevo, very often it is stated that it was Serbs who held these elevations around Sarajevo and that Muslims did not have access to them. In your research, did you actually come across information to the effect that many of the elevations around Sarajevo were actually held by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, many, little, et cetera, that doesn't assist the Chamber. If you say 70 per cent, fine, or if you mention specific ones, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can mention specific ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you mention them and then see if the witness knows anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Colina Kapa is, and do you know that it was in the hands of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and from there there is a view of almost all of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know where it is. I've not specifically taken in the view. I have written at some length in the report about the key elevations, and which side they were on and how they changed hands in the course of the war. I haven't certainly treated them all or this report would be 500 pages long, but I think that the general tenor, the direction of things, is pretty well captured in the paper as it reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you briefly about Grdonja and Hum. From Grdonja you can see Ilidza and Vogosca that were held by Serbs, and from Hum you can see Grbavica and all of Sarajevo including Ilidza; is that correct? And did you know that these two elevations were held by the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, Hum was taken by the ARBiH in May of 1992, and I don't know about the other part that you mentioned, but of course it was a key strategic goal of the ARBiH to take this, say, mid-level high ground both because they wanted it for their own purposes but also to deny it to those who were assaulting the city with infantry or with artillery and tank attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From these elevations the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not only prevent the other side from firing at town but they actually fired at civilian parts of Sarajevo that were held by the Serb forces; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It certainly is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to speed up a bit. The Cutileiro Plan, you say that it failed. You didn't say why it failed. Why did the Cutileiro Plan fail? It was before the conflict, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've indicated in the report, Cutileiro actually submitted a number of plans, proposals, in the course of the first six months of 1992. The first one that was significant in that it won -- looked like it had the possibility of being accepted, was floated in February and parties backed away from it, largely because of the -- some interference on the part of the -- well, the EU objected to the Serb decision to pronounce or declare a constitution of their own. The Cutileiro Plan that most people think about is the one that we've already discussed of 18 March 1992, which I've characterised as an agreement in principle, and the specifics of that plan are actually fully available in the 11th session that was held on that day when there is a very accurate report to the Bosnian Serb Assembly by Karadzic. The -- all three sides eventually backed away from the plan, before subsequent negotiations could be held to move from an agreement in principle to the, let's say, more specifics. The -- I think some -- the -- many people in the EU believed that it was the Muslim or the SDA side that initiated this, and, indeed, they may have been first but eventually all three parties backed away from the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did it work for the other two sides to remain faithful to the plan if the third one wouldn't? You will agree that it didn't make any sense to negotiate any further when the Muslim side did not want to negotiate about that anymore that way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would turn to the words of Karadzic at that 11th session, in which he said, We are not going to agree to anything that we didn't sign. So I think it was the position of all three sides that until that final agreement was reached, it was not a valid agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it the break time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but before we take the break, could I ask one clarification? You asked for many high grounds in the hands of the Army of BiH. You mentioned three. Do I have to understand that this is the position of the Defence, that the significant high grounds were Colina Kapa, Hum hill and Grdonj. Is that how I have to understand it or was it just examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Examples since this gentleman obviously is not capable of knowing all of them or the names. He didn't even recognise Grdonj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but he did recognise the tow other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have Balino Brdo, Brijesce Brdo, Mojmilo, Igman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the position of the Defence as significant high grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't confirm. I just wanted to see if this gentleman took it into account. This was confirmed by the UN witnesses here. There is also Zuc elevation. It's in the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to know what the position of the Defence was in this respect. But it's more than the three you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear, but although you do not put further questions to the witness on that. Then we take a break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber would urge you to see whether you can finish in the next session. We take a break and we'll resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just want to inform you that my estimate is better than my wish. And I estimated 7 hours and I can cut it down but I cannot finish today. Half an hour is not enough. I have to deal now with the second report. It will not be as extensive as the first one but we'll have, I'm afraid, to see Dr. Donia tomorrow, at least for the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider your request to use all the time in accordance with your estimate. But at this moment, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Donia, now I'd like to move on to your report that has to do with the session of the assembly of Republika Srpska, at first the assembly of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, P2001, if I wrote that down correctly. In relation to this, you said in your report that the general first referred on 12 May, the 16th session, but yesterday, or actually on Thursday, the question was that on 25 April 1992, the general took over this position. I'm asking you whether you knew that General Mladic came to Bosnia only on the 9th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He came from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't certain of the exact date but I was aware that he came within a day of that anyway so I certainly accept that representation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Officially he was appointed on the 24th of April but you do know that always a certain period of time elapses before one takes over one's duties. You said that he attended seven assembly sessions until May 1994 and on the 50th session in April, out of a total of 66 sessions that were held, so actually in that light, we will be discussing, this is what you say in the English version in e-court, we need 2001, fourth page, end of the second paragraph; page 5 in B/C/S, end of the first paragraph. As you were explaining why General Mladic did not attend sessions you say despite his frequent absence other senior generals of the VRS attended most sessions and some of their remarks are included in the following highlights. This is what I'd like to ask you. Do you know whether these other military representatives were invited through General Mladic or whether they were invited in their personal capacity, personally? Do you have any information about this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would just briefly like to say a few words about the methodology that you applied in this report. In English it's page 5, the first paragraph, and in B/C/S, it's page 5, the third paragraph there. You say -- the second sentence in this first paragraph: "Excerpting necessarily entails removing a statement from its immediate context but I have sought to retain or explain as much of each statement's context as possible consistent with the principle of reasonable brevity." We do understand and you explained to us that it would have been a huge report if you had taken everything into account. However, the position of our defence is that such a method does not give a full picture regarding the sessions of the assembly or the decisions passed by this assembly, so we are going to show that to you by resorting to a few examples. First example, a conclusion is based on what is said. If one takes only excerpts -- well, we would need page 24 of this paper of yours, the third paragraph in English. It's the 50th session. The 15th and 16th of April, page 33, first paragraph in B/C/S. We see here the words of Mr. Aleksa Buha. This is what he says: "First of all as regards territory, the assembly defined the objectives of this struggle..." it's obvious there is a problem with the page number.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you've given the e-court number and I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's minus 2 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then it's 22nd page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So it should be page 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So page 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, 22 in English. Then it's B/C/S 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so page 22 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Twenty-two in English, yes. Twenty-two in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's item 49, I take it, you're reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is page 22, item 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'll start again: "First of all as regards the territory, the assembly defined the objectives of this struggle in the territorial sense at least globally. However, one deputy said yesterday and another one today that we missed the opportunity of taking Sarajevo, Tuzla, Bihac, et cetera. This, my dear friends, was never the programme of the SDS. I think that this question should not be raised for the single reason that we have not set out to fight a war of conquest but we keep saying that this is a defensive, patriotic defensive war, and secondly that we are not intent on destroying other peoples but want to secure the freedom of our own people on the ethnic territories which are ours." This is this portion, and this is the end of quotation. This is the portion of the contribution and debate. You will agree with me that when you discuss the statements of these other two delegates, criticised by Mr. Buha, had you done that, we would have had a different conclusion and a different impression than the one that we gain by reading what Mr. Buha said.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what conclusion or impression that you are referring to in terms of gaining it from Mr. Buha's statement. It seems to me pretty clear that he is opposed to these other two claims and says so very clearly and emphasises that the nature of the war would have been different had we followed their suggestions. So it seems to me it supports the -- much consistency with other statements which emphasise that this is not a war to conquer all of Bosnia in the eyes of the SDS but was in fact limited by certain territorial objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm precisely asking you this: Had we been able to read the statement of these two delegates, had you selected them instead of Mr. Buha, the picture would have been completely different. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it might have been the same if I'd select them in addition to Mr. Buha's. I chose this because it seemed to me that he was the authoritative figure speaking for the SDS here and there were from time to time these delegates who favoured a more aggressive position for the conquest or for the VRS. And the SDS leaders, including Buha, simply knocked them down, rejected those viewpoints. That's what I was trying to capture here and seems to me it's -- it does so. It refers to the other two and then points out that they are excessive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this eloquent response but I need to ask you again, since you didn't provide an answer: Had you selected and chosen the statements of these two delegates, and we are talking about the selectiveness of your report, had you chosen these two instead of Aleksa Buha, the reader would have gained a completely different impression and would have had a completely different picture.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. If I had selected just those two and not the refutation to it, it would have been different, certainly. It would have been much less representative of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, may I approach my client?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only for a short consultation, low volume.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now briefly look at our second objection. Our second objection is that in your report, you first start with a question that was posed by a delegate but you failed to provide an answer to that question. So on page 71 in English in e-court, paragraph 2, which should correspond to page 69 of your hard copy report, it's item 168, and we are talking about the 32nd session held on the 19th and 20th May 1993. In B/C/S, it's page 96, fourth paragraph. I'm going to read it. I'm quoting from item 168 and this is a speech by Ljubo Bosiljcic, and I quote: "My third question is for General Mladic, and I would ask him to answer before the parliament, who commands the military police? As much as I know, it is outside any command. Military policemen can kill a man whenever they want. They can break into apartments whenever they want. They can use violence whenever they want. Military policemen should be under a single command. They should be responsible for their good and bad actions just like other citizens, and military, judicial organs should work in the way civil judiciary organises do." In your report, I did not manage to find the response by Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, can we have in e-court 65 ter 02378?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you repeat the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 02378.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a minutes of the meeting that you are referring to. I did this in a hurry; therefore, I failed to find the B/C/S version. I only have the English one and we need page 89.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Both versions are on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know which page it is in B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to read a portion in the second paragraph which begins with, "Gentlemen." This is a response as recorded, the response given by General Mladic. It's a lengthy one and this is his answer posed by Delegate Bosiljcic, and it is being recorded that General Mladic said the following, and I quote: [In English] "Gentlemen, I am not satisfied with the level of discipline in the army either, nor am I satisfied with the efficiency of judicial authorities or the police." There is some more, but on the next page, 90, there is continuation, more concrete, about different things. But under number sixth it says, and it is the sixth paragraph on this page, it says: "Sixth, a sweeping campaign should be launched to prevent the abuse of the army, military police, and MUP uniforms. Believe me, true soldiers, true members of the MUP, do not do things you have talked about. Believe me that. It is those who put on various uniforms and do all of -- all sorts of trouble. Even some of you brought certain individuals from distance -- from -- it does then distance myself from such dishonest behaviour." Obviously cut short. It was a long answer: "So a broad campaign should be launched to prevent the abuse of army, military police and MUP uniforms. And the president, the assembly and the government should support the campaign. We cannot do it on our own. Please let us eradicate such behaviour. Let us not allow water to become turbid at the source, be it the Main Staff, the corps, or a brigade. It must be clear everywhere that we are serving our people and we can serve them only if we have honour" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] The last page, yes, page 91, at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, would you agree that only a comprehensive approach can provide a full picture? It's not enough just to quote a question. One needs to see what kind of answer is given to that question.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I would agree that a comprehensive approach can provide a full picture. And I think this is a fair criticism that you're making. One comes up against simply limitations of mass. You know, I would have to say I think that just about every word that General Mladic and Radovan Karadzic said to the assembly in these sessions is meaningful and ideally would be included in a report such as this. I'm limited or constrained only by the considerations of length and I think the ability of a reader to concentrate on a particular issue, I try to limit one excerpt to one particular issue, but that's not a perfect solution. It's very true. I'm glad that you brought this into evidence to show the very spirited response that he gave to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about the ideals and objectives of the Bosnian Serb nationalists. Let's move to page 7 in e-court of the English version. I suppose it's page 5 of your paper. In B/C/S, it's the second paragraph on page 8. English is page 7 in the e-court, paragraph 1. Should be the third sentence in that paragraph. [Interpretation] It's recorded here that Slobodan Bijelic said the following: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We don't have the proper page, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For a long time now there has been a conspiracy into reducing the Serbian people into a national minority. We are not talking about now the constitutional issues. Would it be the case that being outvoted, the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina would actually be deprived of their status of a constituent people by applying the principle of one person/one vote? Did you read anything about what the Serbs referred to "minorisation" of Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina in that period?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I interpret that as essentially what he is saying here is the same thing, and that's why it's part of these excerpts. I'm trying to include those statements which are well expressed that clearly state the position of the Bosnian Serb leadership, and then that can be weighed as to whether it's valid or invalid or -- but at least it's explanatory. It helps explain other parts of their position and the attitude that they were taking toward events at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We talked about this conditional approach by the Serbian side in their future actions and now let's look at paragraph 3 on page 7, and page 9 in B/C/S. It reads, "If we are outvoted ..." I'm sorry, the date of the session is 21 November 1991. These are Mr. Krajisnik's words. He says: "If we are outvoted in discussion of national interests to the Serbian people, the will of the Serbian people will be expressed through the decisions of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina." We see here the conditional approach and the fear of Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina of losing their status of a constituent people and that they would have no say whatsoever in Bosnia-Herzegovina any longer. In your research, have you noticed this fear among the Serbs? Do you find it justified, in terms that, by simply being outvoted would amount to the Serbs being deprived of their status of a constituent people in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My own opinion is it's not justified, but this is, I think, a very precise, concise, accurate statement of exactly what that fear was and what the position of the SDS leadership was and the reason for forming the assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask clarification, whether the fear was justified or not, if you are in a minority politically, would fear to be outvoted, if this has happened before, would that in no way be justified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think some variant of it might be. At this point, the -- at the point that he uttered this, the Serbs had just taken the decisive step of creating their own separate assembly and I think they have excessively focused on the question of outvoting or majority rule as the source of fear for them. I don't think that the -- they had reason to fear the overall political situation as strongly as this statement suggests. That's my personal assessment of it. But I certainly want to, you know, give space for them to express exactly what it was that they opposed and feared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll then ask you the following: You think they had reason to fear the overall political situation. What you say is there was more to fear. Does that in any way undermine any justified fear for a smaller question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I guess what I'm saying is I think they are unnecessarily riveted on this single question of constituent peoples, which was a constitutional principle that they believed applied to a whole bunch of areas that it didn't seem to me it applied to, and so they focused on that one issue to express their fears about. I believe the overall situation created less reason for them to be fearful. And in fact, if you look at the negotiations that were following the statements of the 15th of October, you see a much more flexible approach to dealing with the other two parties than you see here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say they believed that this constitutional principle "applied to a whole bunch of areas that it didn't seem to me it applied to." Every vote in parliament would not be subject to a risk of being outvoted and to be minority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I mean by that is that this is contested. There were so many undecided factors at this point, as I believe Mr. Krajisnik says in the -- one of these entries, I may have taken it out for this, so aptly describes the situation with the council of national equality which had been provided for in the existing constitution including amendments of 1990 but had never actually been operationalised, established, by the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So these discussions hinge on whether a non-existent body should have provided this protection. I can't get to the bottom of that. My constitutional mind has a difficulty with that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I would respond to that, the more reason for fear, if the protective institutions do not function.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand your position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not my position. I'm just putting questions. Not taking any position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I just think that the -- let's put it this way. Some of this certainly was justified. I think they have overstated the threat in this and overestimated the basis for fear in their own positions and responses to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just go back to your initial answer. You were asked about: "In your research, have you noticed this fear among the Serbs? Do you find it justified, in terms that, by ... being outvoted ...," et cetera. Your answer was: "My opinion is it's not justified." As I now understand that some fear may have been justified but perhaps not at the level they expressed it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would -- yes, that's exactly right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we will adjourn for the day. But I would first like to instruct you, Mr. Donia, not to communicate, not to speak or in any other way communicate within about your testimony and we would like to see you back tomorrow morning when we will conclude your testimony. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber, having monitored and having followed the way in which the cross-examination was conducted, gives you tomorrow the first session to complete your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will just have to condense three hours into one but I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would not have had three hours, according to your own estimate, but let's leave it to that. Yes. According to ours, you would have had one hour and ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will finish in the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn for the day and we resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 27th of August, at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, III.
